title: Reading Images: The Grammar of Visual Design (3rd ed.)
key_findings: Systematic social-semiotic 'grammar' of images: representational (narrative vs conceptual), interactive (contact demand/offer, social distance, attitude/angle), modality, compositional (information value given-new / ideal-real / centre-margin, salience, framing).
3rd ed. adds material on diagrams/data visualisation and a new approach to modality; chapters on materiality and the third dimension (publisher page).

Per secondary quotations of the 2006 ed. (p.181): coding orientations are culturally specific on the horizontal axis; in right-to-left writing cultures the given is on the right. KvL (1998:218) admit the epistemological status of their claim is the major challenge.
practical_applications: Vocabulary for briefing and critique: name what each slide/frame does (demand vs offer, given vs new, framing strength).
limitations: Theory from analyst readings, not experiments.
Book content not read this session beyond publisher listing; framework details from it and secondary sources.

title: Educating the eye? Kress and Van Leeuwen's Reading Images: The Grammar of Visual Design (1996)
key_findings: Review praises innovative, bold proposals but discusses weaknesses that follow from the semiotic/ideological approach: classification and interpretation of images and how far the concepts generalise.
Suggests links to the emerging cognitivist paradigm.
practical_applications: Treat KvL categories as analytic lenses, not laws; check generalisation per genre/culture.
limitations: Only abstract read.

title: Reading paths and visual perception in multimodal research, psychology and brain sciences
key_findings: Argues the multimodal concept of 'reading path' is not sufficiently reliable for lack of empirical testing.
Notes Holsanova & Holmqvist eye-tracking gave only limited support to influential social-semiotic reading-path hypotheses (KvL).
Eye-movement research contradicts a separate 'scanning then reading' stage; perception is task-driven (Yarbus, Rayner).
van Leeuwen (1993) listed three needed inputs: cultural reading direction, perceptual salience, semantic factors that may override salience (e.g. the human figure).
practical_applications: Design reading paths as hypotheses and test them (eye-tracking, heat data, or at least a 5-viewer first-look test).
limitations: Methodological position paper; no new data.

title: Entry points and reading paths on newspaper spreads: comparing a semiotic analysis with eye-tracking measurements
authors: Jana Holsanova; Henrik Rahm; Kenneth Holmqvist
key_findings: Semiotic predictions about a newspaper spread compared with eye-tracking (order of attention, dwell time, reading depth).
Data confirm some assumptions only; five participants showed three reader types: editorial, overview, focused readers.
Quoted in Hiippala2012: readers do not scan the semiotic space before taking a closer look at certain units.
practical_applications: Expect different reader types; a layout must work for skimmers and committed readers.
limitations: n=5; one spread; newspapers not social feeds.

title: The role of local design factors for newspaper reading behaviour - an eye-tracking perspective (LUCS 127)
key_findings: Pictures attract earlier attention than picture-less areas: 'perhaps the most stable result in all types of images' in newspaper eye-tracking.
Large pictures looked at significantly earlier than medium/small ones.
Attention concentrates just left of the spread's middle; when ads are excluded the leftward dominance disappears, i.e. texts read independently of position.
Larger texts are looked at longer but not read deeper (Hansen's rule cited: triple length -> half reading depth).
Readers do not all start top-left; they switch between texts and pictures.
practical_applications: Image first, then short text; size is the strongest lever for entry point; do not rely on 'left = read first' alone.
limitations: Authors call it a case study, not a controlled experiment; Swedish newspapers.

title: Reading information graphics: The role of spatial contiguity and dual attentional guidance
authors: Jana Holsanova; Nils Holmberg; Kenneth Holmqvist
key_findings: Integrated format (text placed next to the picture part it explains) facilitates integration.
Serial format with dual scripting (layout suggests a reading path + conceptual pre-structuring) significantly enhances reading; attracts and sustains attention, deeper processing.
practical_applications: Put each caption next to the image part it refers to; number steps in an explainer carousel.
limitations: Newspaper info graphics, Swedish readers; online 2008, print 2009.

title: A system for image-text relations in new (and old) media
key_findings: Generalised system combining (1) relative status of image and text and (2) logico-semantic relations, building on Barthes and Halliday (secondary sources: equal status split into independent/complementary; logico-semantics elaboration/extension/enhancement, projection).
Units and realisations specified for human analysts and machines.
practical_applications: Label each text-image pair: does the line restate (elaborate), add (extend), give time/cause/place (enhance) or voice/thought (project)?
limitations: Abstract only; sub-category details from secondary sources.

title: Rhetoric of the Image (in Image-Music-Text, trans. S. Heath; French original 1964)
key_findings: Linguistic message relates to the image as anchorage (text fixes one of the image's possible meanings; common in press photos and ads) or relay (text and image complementary, text supplies what the image lacks; typical of cartoons/comics).
Panzani ad analysis: connoted 'Italianicity'.
practical_applications: Ads/product posts: caption anchors; story carousels: dialogue relays.
limitations: Semiotic essay, not empirical. Read this session only via course summaries (registry holds full text).

title: Text and Image: A Critical Introduction to the Visual/Verbal Divide
key_findings: Survey of text-image approaches: socio-semiotics, visual communication, psycholinguistic discourse, rhetoric of advertising, cognitive metaphor; applied to ads, picture books, comics, textbooks.
practical_applications: Reference for choosing a text-image framework by genre.
limitations: Only publisher/catalogue pages read.

title: A multimodal discourse theory of visual narrative
key_findings: Extends Segmented Discourse Representation Theory to visual narrative (discourse-pragmatic inference between panels).
Reported by Cohn (2018) as arguing that a grammar for sequential images is unnecessary.
practical_applications: Alternative to Cohn's grammar: panels linked by discourse relations (inference) rather than syntax.
limitations: Search summary only.

title: Art and Visual Perception: A Psychology of the Creative Eye (The New Version)
key_findings: Gestalt account of art: perception organises visual material by psychological premises; chapter 1 'Balance' with 'The Structural Skeleton' of the frame (axes and centre).
First edition 1954; revised 1974.
practical_applications: Vocabulary of visual forces, balance, structural skeleton for critique.
limitations: Primary text not read; contents via publisher and secondary sources.

title: A Primer of Visual Literacy
key_findings: Treats composition principles as 'syntactical guidelines for visual literacy' (per a CUNY course reading); builds from basic elements to combinations and finished works (publisher description).
practical_applications: Historical root of 'visual literacy' and visual syntax as teachable.
limitations: Bibliographic and secondary descriptions only.

title: Arnheim's Gestalt theory of visual balance: Examining the compositional structure of art photographs and abstract images
authors: I. C. McManus; Katharina Stöver; Do Kim
key_findings: Art photographs' centre of mass slightly more often on a symmetry axis than random photos (46.6% vs 39.7%, p=.028); people's crops too.
When only CoM position changed, no preference for on-axis (48.4%, n.s.); in another study a significant preference for the off-axis image (42.6% on-axis).
Physicalist reading of Arnheim's balance not supported; features driving preference unidentified.
practical_applications: Do not justify a layout by 'centre of mass balance'; test real versions.
limitations: Subtle stimulus differences; one book of art photos.

title: Mapping the perceptual structure of rectangles through goodness-of-fit ratings
key_findings: Probe-fit ratings at 77 positions highest at centre, elevated along vertical/horizontal symmetry axes and local symmetry axes; six symmetry factors explained 95% of variance.
Dividing a frame into subframes makes position within the local subframe the main determinant.
Consistent with Arnheim's structural skeleton, but explainable by Gestalt figural goodness.
practical_applications: Split-screen/panel layouts create new local skeletons: compose inside each panel.
limitations: Fit ratings for a circle, not complex images.

title: The Attentional Theory of Cinematic Continuity
key_findings: Continuity is a viewer outcome: CE rules use natural attentional cues (off-screen sound, conversational turns, motion, gaze, pointing) pre-cut and match minimal expectations post-cut.
Over 90% of surveyed Hollywood shots follow CE rules (citing Bordwell et al. 1985; Levin & Wang 2009).
Match-action cuts hardest to detect: about a third missed in a cut-detection task (Smith & Henderson 2008).
Levin & Simons 1997: only 33% noticed an actor swap across a matched exit/entrance.
practical_applications: Cut on motion/gaze; put the post-cut target where the eye already is; keep spatiotemporal continuity of characters.
limitations: Theory plus selected evidence; mostly Western narrative film.

title: Edit Blindness: The relationship between attention and global change blindness in dynamic scenes
authors: Tim J. Smith; John M. Henderson
doi_isbn: Journal of Eye Movement Research (as cited in Smith2012)
key_findings: As reported in Smith2012: match-action cuts were the hardest cut type to detect; about one third missed.
practical_applications: Hide cuts inside actions.
limitations: Not read this session; cited via Smith2012.

title: The impact of continuity editing in narrative film on event segmentation
authors: Joseph P. Magliano; Jeffrey M. Zacks
key_findings: The Red Balloon, 211 edits coded: continuity (111), spatial-temporal discontinuity (81), action discontinuity (19).
Action discontinuities had the biggest impact on event segmentation (coarse regression weight 0.96); spatial/temporal jumps had small or no effect; continuity edits raised only fine segmentation.
fMRI: regions that increased at edits and decreased at action discontinuities interpreted as bridging visual discontinuities while keeping action continuity.
practical_applications: A new 'scene' for viewers = a change of action/goal, not a change of camera; place boundaries (slide changes, chapter cards) at action changes.
limitations: One film; n=41 and 24; fMRI interpretation is reverse inference.

title: Event perception: A mind-brain perspective
authors: Jeffrey M. Zacks; Nicole K. Speer; Khena M. Swallow; Todd S. Braver; Jeremy R. Reynolds
key_findings: Event Segmentation Theory: perceptual systems predict what happens next; transient prediction errors are perceived as event boundaries, which regulate attention and memory.
Event perception uses sensory cues and knowledge of event parts and actors' goals.
practical_applications: Make each slide/shot either continue the prediction (mapping) or break it on purpose (boundary, punchline).
limitations: Abstract read.

title: The Scene Perception & Event Comprehension Theory (SPECT) applied to visual narratives
authors: Lester C. Loschky; Adam M. Larson; Tim J. Smith; Joseph P. Magliano
key_findings: Front-end (within a fixation: attentional selection, information extraction) vs back-end (event model in working memory: laying foundation, mapping, shifting).
Missing bridging image in a picture story -> longer viewing, about 20% more fixations (not longer fixations), aimed at inference-relevant regions (Magliano et al. 2016; Hutson et al. 2018).
'Tyranny of film': edited film produces high attentional synchrony; event-model differences barely change gaze except in a static, motion-free shot; a map-drawing task can reduce it.
Self-paced static narratives allow more back-end influence on gaze than film.
practical_applications: Carousels (self-paced) can leave gaps for inference; clips (fast, motion) must steer attention explicitly.
limitations: Largely the authors' own lab studies; Western stimuli.

title: The Visual Language of Comics: Introduction to the Structure and Cognition of Sequential Images
key_findings: Drawings and sequential images structured like language: lexicon of stored patterns, combination strategies, hierarchic narrative grammar; cross-cultural visual languages.
practical_applications: Treat a series style as a 'visual vocabulary' to keep stable.
limitations: Abstract only; strong claim contested (Bateman & Wildfeuer 2014).

title: The grammar of visual narrative: Neural evidence for constituent structure in sequential image comprehension
authors: Neil Cohn; Ray Jackendoff; Phillip J. Holcomb; Gina R. Kuperberg
key_findings: Blank panels inside a narrative constituent (vs at its boundary) evoked a left anterior negativity (500-700 ms); inside the second constituent also a P600.
Suggests readers build hierarchic constituents in wordless strips, similar to syntax.
practical_applications: Put pauses/beat panels at constituent boundaries, not mid-sequence.
limitations: n=24; some marginal effects; Peanuts strips; one lab.

title: Your brain on comics: a cognitive model of visual narrative comprehension
key_findings: Parallel Interfacing Narrative-Semantics (PINS) model; details in creative-intelligence/knowledge/cartoon/COMICS_AND_SEQUENTIAL_ART.md.
practical_applications: See M44 file.
limitations: Not re-read this session; cited for linkage only.

title: How readers navigate comic book pages: evidence from eye movements
authors: Paul A. Aleixo; Jane L. Morgan; Diarmuid B. Verrier
key_findings: 90 participants, textless Watchmen page: Z-path is an accurate prototype of panel order but with much variation.
Only 49% first fixated panel 1; panel 1->2 transition 58%; after panel 2, 43% went on to panel 3 and 34% back to panel 1 (regressions, read by authors as context checking).
Previous Z-path evidence was limited to self-report.
practical_applications: Z-order works as a default for grids, but expect back-checks: repeat key cues across adjacent panels.
limitations: One page, 9-panel grid, no text; UK sample.

title: Understanding Comics: The Invisible Art
key_findings: Craft theory of closure in the gutter and six panel-transition types (see cartoon/COMICS_AND_SEQUENTIAL_ART.md).
practical_applications: Planning vocabulary for transitions.
limitations: Craft, not evidence; Cohn critiques transition theory.

title: Film Art: An Introduction
key_findings: Standard textbook of film form, mise-en-scene, cinematography, editing (continuity system); quoted in Smith2012: continuity editing aims to tell a story coherently with a smooth flow from shot to shot.
practical_applications: Shared vocabulary for 16:9 story scenes.
limitations: Not read this session.

title: Meaning-based guidance of attention in scenes as revealed by meaning maps
authors: John M. Henderson; Taylor R. Hayes
key_findings: 40 scenes; meaning (crowd-rated patches, 165 raters) and saliency correlated r=0.80.
Meaning explained 53% vs saliency 38% of fixation-density variance; unique variance 19% vs 4% (n.s. for saliency).
Meaning advantage present from the first fixation.
practical_applications: The eye goes to what is informative (face, hands, the product), not only to bright spots.
limitations: Free-viewing tasks; meaning maps' validity disputed (Pedziwiatr2021).

title: Meaning maps and saliency models based on deep convolutional neural networks are insensitive to image meaning when predicting human fixations
authors: Marek A. Pedziwiatr; Matthias Kümmerer; Thomas S. A. Wallis; Matthias Bethge; Christoph Teufel
key_findings: Deep saliency model DeepGaze II predicted fixations better than meaning maps; neither responded to meaning manipulations that changed human gaze.
Argues meaning maps index visual features; Henderson's group replied; debate continues.
practical_applications: Neither 'salience' nor 'meaning' maps alone predict the eye; test real viewers.
limitations: Search summary only.

title: How saliency, faces, and sound influence gaze in dynamic social scenes
key_findings: In conversation videos, viewers look more at faces, especially talking faces, regardless of soundtrack; the original soundtrack makes gaze follow speech turn-taking more closely.
Classical saliency models fail in conversation scenes without face and sound terms.
practical_applications: In dialogue scenes the speaking character is the attention anchor; voice and mouth cues steer gaze.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: F-Shaped Pattern of Reading on the Web: Misunderstood, But Still Relevant (Even on Mobile)
key_findings: F-pattern occurs when three conditions hold: little formatting (wall of text), user wants efficiency, user not committed to read every word; default when no strong cues guide the eye.
Mirrored in Arabic; also seen on mobile.
Considered bad for users and businesses; antidotes: key points first, informative headings starting with key words, bold, lists.
practical_applications: F-pattern is a failure mode of text pages, not a layout to imitate.
limitations: Commercial UX research; heatmap samples ~45-47 users; method details limited.

title: Text Scanning Patterns: Eyetracking Evidence
key_findings: Four patterns: F, spotted, layer-cake (most effective), commitment; driven by task, prior experience, layout/content type, motivation, efficiency.
practical_applications: Design caption/subtitle text for layer-cake and spotted scanning: strong headings, distinctive key words.
limitations: Web text, not images; commercial.

title: Directional bias in the mental representation of spatial events: Nature or culture?
key_findings: Italians drew sentence subject left of object; Arabs reversed (right).
Picture-sentence matching faster when subject in script-typical position; plus a language-independent facilitation for left-to-right action, suggesting both hemispheric and scanning-habit factors.
practical_applications: For left-to-right readers (Thai, English), agent-on-left and motion left-to-right read as default/forward; reversing it is a marked choice.
limitations: Abstract read; lab tasks with simple drawings.

title: Spatial agency bias review (Advances in Experimental Social Psychology vol. 53, pp. 245-301)
key_findings: As described by citing papers: agency represented on the left with left-to-right trajectory in rightward-script cultures; reverses in right-to-left cultures; script and visuo-motor accounts.
practical_applications: Who is placed left/right and which way they move carries agency connotations.
limitations: Known only via citing papers; exact chapter title not verified.

title: Reading and writing direction effects on the aesthetic appreciation of photographs
authors: Sobh Chahboun; Andrea Flumini; Carmen Pérez González; I. Chris McManus; Julio Santiago
key_findings: Spanish (L-R) vs Moroccan (R-L) viewers: no directional effect in single ratings (Exp 1); in paired original-vs-mirror choice, Spaniards preferred rightward and Moroccans leftward versions (Exp 2).
Effect appears when people attend to the lateral dimension; not moderated by model sex.
practical_applications: Mirror-flipping a picture is mostly harmless for single viewing but matters when versions are compared or direction is salient.
limitations: Abstract read.

title: Cross-cultural and developmental trends in graphic productions
authors: Barbara Tversky; Sol Kugelmass; Atalia Winter
key_findings: About 1200 English, Hebrew, Arabic speakers: writing direction affected only temporal representations (L-R English, R-L Arabic, Hebrew between); quantity and preference used all directions except top-to-bottom about equally; more/better mapped upward.
practical_applications: Timelines and before/after go left-to-right for Thai readers; 'more/better = up' is safer than left/right for value.
limitations: Abstract read.

title: How the eyes connect to the heart: The influence of eye gaze direction on advertising effectiveness
authors: Rita Ngoc To; Vanessa M. Patrick; Margaret C. Campbell; JoAndrea Hoegg
key_findings: Five experiments incl. a Facebook field study: averted model gaze increases narrative transportation and effectiveness of emotional ads; direct gaze better for informational ads (credibility) and when viewers do not want to identify with negative emotion.
practical_applications: KvL 'demand' (direct gaze) is not automatically stronger; choose gaze by appeal type.
limitations: Abstract read; author list varies across indexes (IDEAS lists four).

title: The influence of banner advertisements on attention and memory: human faces with averted gaze can enhance advertising effectiveness
key_findings: Faces with averted gaze in banners increased attention to the banner, its text and product, and improved memory for brand and message; mutual gaze localised attention on the face, weakening memory benefit.
practical_applications: If a model looks at the viewer, the product loses looks; aim the gaze at the product when the product is the message.
limitations: Banner ads on web pages; abstract read.

title: Eye movements when reading spaced and unspaced Thai and English: A comparison of Thai-English bilinguals and English monolinguals
authors: Heather Winskel; Ralph Radach; Sudaporn Luksaneeyanawin
key_findings: In Thai, interword spaces facilitated word recognition but did not change eye guidance or landing positions; removing spaces severely disrupted English reading.
practical_applications: Thai overlay text: short phrases with line breaks at word boundaries help recognition.
limitations: Abstract text seen via search summary; sentence reading, not image overlays.

title: Design Tokens Specification 2025.10 (Format, Color, Resolver modules)
key_findings: Design tokens = indivisible pieces of a design system such as colours, spacing, typography scale; first stable version 2025.10 (28 Oct 2025); Community Group report, not a W3C Standard.
practical_applications: Store a series' visual constants (palette, type scale, margins, line weight) as named tokens read by HTML templates.
limitations: Index page read; module details not read.

title: Atomic Design
key_findings: Atoms -> molecules -> organisms -> templates -> pages; templates are layout skeletons, pages are templates with real content.
practical_applications: Model a carousel system: tokens/atoms (colour, type), molecules (bubble+name), organisms (panel), template (4-slide layout), page (one story).
limitations: Craft method; secondary summaries read.

title: Instagram carousels engagement study (Socialinsider data, reported by Search Engine Journal)
key_findings: Reported: 22M posts; carousels 1.92% engagement vs 1.74% images, 1.45% video; most carousels 2-4 slides; 10-slide highest; 'swipe' prompts 1.83%->2%.
practical_applications: Weak hint only: carousel format is not penalised; test slide count yourself.
limitations: Vendor data, methodology unknown, correlational; year not confirmed; secondary report.
